P8-T6.claude:
[{"title":"Internal walk-away number disclosed to opposing counsel","body":"<NARRATIVE_REVIEWER_MEMO>
Issue: The settlement letter discloses the client's internal walk-away number to opposing counsel. This is a BLOCKER for responsible attorney release. The walk-away number is the client's confidential reservation price—the lowest amount the client will accept (or highest it will pay). Revealing it to the adverse party destroys negotiating leverage: opposing counsel will simply anchor to that figure, and the stated 50/50 offer becomes meaningless because the other side now knows the true floor/ceiling.

Source basis: Matter context expressly states the letter 'additionally states the client's internal walk-away number' and is 'addressed to opposing counsel.' The 50/50 split is identified as a final, locked business decision and is NOT the subject of this critique—I am not reopening the split. The walk-away disclosure is a separate defect from the locked settlement-amount decision.

Jurisdiction: This is not jurisdiction-dependent substantive law; it is a drafting/confidentiality error common to Virginia and Maryland practice. However, note that settlement communications are generally protected from admissibility under Va. Code / Va. R. Evid. 2:408 and Md. Rule 5-408, but that evidentiary protection does NOT cure the strategic harm of voluntarily handing the adverse party your reservation price. Rule 408 protects against courtroom use, not against your opponent exploiting the number at the bargaining table.

Why this is DRAFTING, not BUSINESS: The attorney has already made the business decision (50/50). Whether to concede on amount is settled. The presence of the internal walk-away number is not a chosen negotiating position—it is almost certainly an inadvertent inclusion (e.g., carried over from an internal client memo or negotiation-strategy note). Removing confidential internal strategy from an outbound adversary letter is a question of how to express the settled position, so this is SUBSTANTIVE/DRAFTING. I am not choosing a settlement number for the attorney.

Recommended action: Strike the walk-away number entirely from the outbound letter before sending. Confirm no other internal strategy content (BATNA, litigation-cost estimates, client's emotional posture, authority limits) survived into the draft. Verify the version sent to opposing counsel is segregated from any internal strategy memo.

Attorney decision points: (1) Confirm the walk-away number was not intentionally disclosed as a strategic concession; if intentional, that is a BUSINESS decision the attorney owns and I defer. (2) Confirm no residual internal-strategy language remains.
</NARRATIVE_REVIEWER_MEMO>

<issue>The governing-law clause states the agreement is 'governed by the laws of the State of California,' but the matter context identifies this as a Virginia purchase and sale agreement. This is a facial inconsistency between the chosen governing law and the transaction's apparent situs/jurisdiction. Before release, this must be reconciled: either the California choice is intentional (and defensible) or it is a drafting/template carryover error.</issue>
<source_basis>Document text (governing-law clause naming California) read against provided matter context ('A Virginia purchase and sale agreement').</source_basis>
<jurisdiction_treatment>The reviewer cannot confirm from the record whether California law was deliberately selected. Two distinct jurisdictional concerns arise and should be separated:

(1) Enforceability of the California choice-of-law clause. If the property and parties are Virginia-connected, a Virginia court applying Virginia conflicts rules will generally enforce a contractual choice of law only where the chosen state bears a reasonable relationship to the transaction and application would not offend Virginia public policy. Virginia follows lex loci for many contract questions and, critically, real property is generally governed by the law of the situs (lex rei sitae). For a PSA conveying Virginia real property, Virginia (situs) law will typically control conveyance, title, recording, and many remedy questions regardless of a contrary contractual choice, so a blanket California choice may be partially ineffective and misleading as to the parties' actual rights.

(2) Maryland is not implicated on the current facts; flagged only to note that if any party or property is Maryland-connected, a parallel situs analysis under Maryland law would apply and should be run separately. Jurisdiction uncertainty is expressly flagged: the record does not state why California appears.</jurisdiction_treatment>
<recommended_action>Confirm with the attorney whether the California designation is intentional. If it is a template carryover (most likely given the Virginia matter context), conform the governing-law clause to Virginia. If California was intended, confirm a reasonable relationship exists and paper the file accordingly, and separately address that Virginia situs law will still govern the real-property conveyance aspects. This is a substance issue, not tone.</recommended_action>
<attorney_decision_points>Whether California law was intentionally selected; if so, the factual basis for a reasonable relationship; and whether a situs-carveout for the real-property conveyance provisions is desired.</attorney_decision_points>
</NARRATIVE_REVIEWER_MEMO>
